title: Cardiac cycle
summary: One heartbeat: relax and fill, then squeeze and eject.

layers.basics: Each heartbeat has two phases: the heart relaxes and fills with blood, then it squeezes to push blood out. This takes under a second.
layers.deeper: The beat begins in the SA node. Pressure differences open and close the valves, creating the 'lub-dub' sounds.
layers.expert: Phases: atrial systole, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid and reduced filling. LV pressure peaks ≈ 120 mmHg; end-diastolic volume ≈ 120 mL, end-systolic ≈ 50 mL; Wiggers diagram links ECG, pressures and volumes.

did_you_know: The heart's four phases occur in under one second, and its valves open and close about 100,000 times daily.

steps.title: Electrical start
steps.text: The SA node in the right atrium fires, and the wave of excitation spreads across both atria.

steps.title: Atria squeeze
steps.text: The atria contract and top up the ventricles with the last 20-30% of their filling.

steps.title: Pause at the AV node
steps.text: The impulse is delayed about 0.1 s at the AV node so the ventricles can fill, then races down the septum and Purkinje fibers.

steps.title: Ventricles tense
steps.text: Ventricular contraction raises pressure; the AV valves slam shut ('lub') while all valves are briefly closed.

steps.title: Ejection
steps.text: When ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the aortic and pulmonary valves open and blood is ejected.

steps.title: Relaxation
steps.text: The ventricles relax, the semilunar valves close ('dub'), and pressure falls.

steps.title: Filling and coronary flow
steps.text: The AV valves open and blood flows in; the coronary arteries fill mainly now.

title: Breathing and gas exchange
summary: Muscles move air in and out; oxygen and carbon dioxide swap with the blood in the alveoli.

layers.basics: To breathe in, the diaphragm contracts and the chest expands, drawing air into the lungs. Oxygen crosses into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves, then you breathe out.
layers.deeper: Pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure when the chest expands, so air flows in. Exhalation at rest is passive recoil.
layers.expert: Boyle's law drives ventilation. Alveolar PO2 ≈ 100 mmHg and PCO2 ≈ 40 mmHg; venous blood arrives at PO2 ≈ 40 and equilibrates in ≈ 0.25 s. Hemoglobin carries ≈ 98% of O2; CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate. Brainstem chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO2/pH.

did_you_know: Red blood cells spend less than a second in a pulmonary capillary, yet that's enough to fully load oxygen.

steps.title: Inspiration
steps.text: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and external intercostals lift the ribs; lung volume grows and pressure drops.

steps.title: Air travels down
steps.text: Air is warmed and filtered through the nose, then passes through larynx, trachea and bronchi.

steps.title: Reaching the alveoli
steps.text: Branching bronchioles deliver fresh air to millions of alveoli.

steps.title: Diffusion across the barrier
steps.text: O2 diffuses into capillary blood and CO2 diffuses out, across a barrier thinner than a micrometer.

steps.title: Oxygen transport
steps.text: Oxygen binds to hemoglobin in red cells and is carried to tissues, which release it where CO2 and acidity are higher.

steps.title: Expiration
steps.text: Muscles relax, elastic recoil of lungs pushes air out carrying CO2.

steps.title: Brain control
steps.text: The brainstem measures blood CO2 and pH and adjusts breathing rate and depth.

title: Action potential (nerve impulse)
summary: A brief, self-propagating electrical pulse that carries signals along a neuron.

layers.basics: A neuron at rest is electrically charged. When stimulated enough, a spike of voltage races down its axon like a wave.
layers.deeper: Sodium channels open, sodium rushes in and flips the voltage; then potassium channels open and restore it. Myelin makes the signal jump quickly.
layers.expert: Threshold ≈ -55 mV, peak ≈ +30 mV, resting ≈ -70 mV; Hodgkin-Huxley kinetics; Na+ channel inactivation gives refractory period; saltatory conduction at nodes of Ranvier reaches ≈ 100 m/s in large myelinated axons.

did_you_know: Despite the electrical name, the 'wire' is salty water, and ions, not electrons, carry the signal.

steps.title: Resting state
steps.text: Na+/K+ pumps and leak channels hold the inside about 70 mV negative.

steps.title: Reaching threshold
steps.text: Incoming inputs depolarize the axon hillock; at about -55 mV voltage-gated Na+ channels open.

steps.title: Rising phase
steps.text: Na+ floods in, reversing the voltage to about +30 mV.

steps.title: Falling phase
steps.text: Na+ channels inactivate and K+ channels open; K+ leaves and the membrane repolarizes.

steps.title: Refractory period
steps.text: Overshoot below rest briefly prevents another spike so the impulse travels one way.

steps.title: Propagation
steps.text: Local currents depolarize the next patch; myelinated axons jump between nodes of Ranvier.

title: Synaptic transmission
summary: How one neuron passes a message to the next using chemicals.

layers.basics: An electrical pulse reaching a nerve ending triggers release of chemical messengers that cross a tiny gap and excite or inhibit the next cell.
layers.deeper: Calcium entering the terminal makes vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter, which binds receptors on the target cell. Chemical synapses can strengthen or weaken with use.
layers.expert: Vesicle fusion via SNARE complexes and synaptotagmin (Ca2+ sensor) takes ≈ 0.2-0.5 ms; ionotropic (AMPA, NMDA, GABA-A) versus metabotropic receptors; reuptake and enzymatic degradation terminate signals; LTP/LTD underlie plasticity.

did_you_know: A single cortical neuron can receive thousands of synaptic inputs.

steps.title: Arrival
steps.text: An action potential reaches the axon terminal.

steps.title: Calcium entry
steps.text: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ rushes in.

steps.title: Release
steps.text: Vesicles fuse with the membrane and spill neurotransmitter into the cleft.

steps.title: Binding
steps.text: Neurotransmitter molecules bind receptors on the next cell, opening ion channels.

steps.title: Response
steps.text: Excitatory inputs depolarize, inhibitory ones hyperpolarize the receiving cell.

steps.title: Cleanup
steps.text: Neurotransmitter is taken back up or broken down; astrocytes help clear excess.

title: Muscle contraction (sliding filament)
summary: Muscle shortens when myosin heads pull actin filaments past them, powered by ATP.

layers.basics: A nerve signal causes calcium to flood the muscle fiber, letting tiny protein motors pull and the muscle tighten.
layers.deeper: Calcium binds troponin, uncovering binding sites on actin; myosin heads attach, pivot and release, powered by ATP.
layers.expert: Excitation-contraction coupling: ACh at the neuromuscular junction → sarcolemma AP → T-tubules → DHPR/RyR1 → Ca2+ release from SR; cross-bridge cycle with ≈ 5-10 nm power stroke; ATP binding detaches heads (rigor mortis lacks ATP).

did_you_know: Rigor mortis happens because dead muscle cannot make ATP to release myosin heads.

steps.title: Nerve signal
steps.text: A motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.

steps.title: Muscle action potential
steps.text: The signal spreads along the membrane and down T-tubules.

steps.title: Calcium release
steps.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+ into the cell.

steps.title: Unlocking actin
steps.text: Ca2+ binds troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites.

steps.title: Cross-bridge cycling
steps.text: Myosin heads attach, swing (power stroke) and detach with ATP; the cycle repeats.

steps.title: Shortening
steps.text: Thin filaments slide inward and sarcomeres shorten, adding up to muscle force.

steps.title: Relaxation
steps.text: Ca2+ is pumped back by SERCA; sites are covered; the muscle relaxes.

title: Digestion and absorption
summary: Food is mechanically and chemically broken into nutrients that cross the gut lining into the body.

layers.basics: Chewing, stomach acid and enzymes break food into tiny molecules, which the small intestine absorbs into the blood.
layers.deeper: Digestion begins in the mouth with amylase, continues in the stomach with acid and pepsin, and finishes in the small intestine with pancreatic enzymes and bile.
layers.expert: Carbohydrates become monosaccharides (SGLT1, GLUT5), proteins become amino acids and di/tripeptides, fats are emulsified by bile, hydrolyzed by lipase into monoglycerides and fatty acids, then repackaged as chylomicrons into lacteals. Hormonal regulation via gastrin, secretin, CCK.

did_you_know: Most of the water your gut handles is actually secretions: about 8-9 L a day, nearly all reabsorbed.

steps.title: Chewing and saliva
steps.text: Teeth grind food while salivary amylase starts splitting starch.

steps.title: Swallowing
steps.text: The tongue pushes food back and peristalsis carries it down the esophagus.

steps.title: Stomach
steps.text: Acid and pepsin break down proteins and the wall churns food into chyme.

steps.title: Bile and enzymes
steps.text: In the duodenum, bile from the liver/gallbladder emulsifies fat and pancreatic enzymes digest all food types.

steps.title: Absorption
steps.text: Villi absorb sugars and amino acids into blood and fats into lymph.

steps.title: Liver processing
steps.text: Portal blood brings nutrients to the liver for storage and processing.

steps.title: Water and microbes
steps.text: The large intestine absorbs water and ferments fiber with the help of microbes.

title: Urine formation in the nephron
summary: The kidney filters blood, reclaims what the body needs, and sends the rest out as urine.

layers.basics: Blood is filtered into the nephron, then useful water and nutrients are taken back and wastes stay in.
layers.deeper: Three steps: filtration at the glomerulus, reabsorption along the tubule, and secretion of extra wastes.
layers.expert: GFR ≈ 120 mL/min; PCT reabsorbs ≈ 65%; loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient; distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune under aldosterone and ADH; final urine ≈ 1 mL/min.

did_you_know: You filter the equivalent of your whole blood plasma about 60 times a day.

steps.title: Filtration
steps.text: Pressure pushes plasma through the glomerular filter into Bowman's capsule; cells and large proteins stay in blood.

steps.title: Bulk reclaim
steps.text: The proximal tubule takes back ≈ 65% of water and salts and nearly all glucose and amino acids.

steps.title: Building a gradient
steps.text: The loop of Henle pumps salt to make the inner kidney very salty.

steps.title: Fine adjustment
steps.text: The distal tubule adjusts Na+, K+, Ca2+ and acid under hormonal control.

steps.title: Water control
steps.text: In the collecting duct, ADH decides how much water leaves, concentrating the urine.

steps.title: Drainage
steps.text: Urine flows through the renal pelvis, ureters, to the bladder and out.

title: Blood clotting (hemostasis)
summary: A cascade that plugs a damaged vessel with platelets and a fibrin mesh.

layers.basics: When a vessel is cut, platelets clump to plug it and proteins build a mesh that seals the wound.
layers.deeper: Hemostasis has three stages: vessel constriction, platelet plug, and coagulation producing fibrin.
layers.expert: Collagen exposure activates platelets (GPVI, α2β1); tissue factor-FVIIa initiates the cascade, thrombin amplifies it via FV, FVIII, FXI, and converts fibrinogen to fibrin; FXIII cross-links; antithrombin and protein C limit the clot; plasmin lyses it.

did_you_know: Hemophilia results from deficiency of a single clotting factor such as factor VIII or IX.

steps.title: Vessel spasm
steps.text: Smooth muscle in the damaged vessel constricts to slow blood loss.

steps.title: Platelets stick
steps.text: Platelets adhere to exposed collagen and become activated.

steps.title: Platelet plug
steps.text: Activated platelets recruit more platelets, forming a loose plug.

steps.title: Cascade
steps.text: Clotting factors trigger a cascade culminating in thrombin.

steps.title: Fibrin mesh
steps.text: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin threads that trap cells.

steps.title: Dissolving the clot
steps.text: After healing, plasmin breaks down the clot.

title: Immune response
summary: Layered defenses: barriers, rapid innate cells, and slower adaptive memory cells.

layers.basics: First your skin blocks germs; if they get in, fast cells attack; and specialized cells learn the invader so next time you respond faster.
layers.deeper: The innate response (inflammation, phagocytes, complement) is immediate and generic. The adaptive response (T and B cells) takes days but is specific and creates memory, which is the basis of vaccines.
layers.expert: PRR recognition (TLRs) triggers cytokine release; dendritic cells present antigen on MHC to naive T cells in lymph nodes; clonal expansion; Th1/Th2/Th17 subsets; B cells undergo affinity maturation; primary response peaks ≈ 7-14 d, secondary within days.

did_you_know: Vaccines work by giving your adaptive immune system a safe preview.

steps.title: Barriers
steps.text: Skin, mucus and stomach acid block most microbes.

steps.title: Innate alarm
steps.text: Macrophages and neutrophils sense microbes, engulf them and release signals that cause inflammation.

steps.title: Antigen presentation
steps.text: Dendritic cells and macrophages carry fragments to lymph nodes.

steps.title: T-cell activation
steps.text: Matching T cells multiply; helper T cells coordinate, killer T cells destroy infected cells.

steps.title: Antibody production
steps.text: B cells, aided by helper T cells, become plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

steps.title: Clearing and memory
steps.text: Pathogens are cleared; memory T and B cells remain for faster future response.

title: Hormone signaling and negative feedback (blood glucose)
summary: Glands release hormones that change body conditions; the change then switches the release off.

layers.basics: After a meal, blood sugar rises, and the pancreas releases insulin to lower it. If sugar falls, glucagon raises it. This keeps sugar steady.
layers.deeper: Insulin helps cells (muscle, fat, liver) take up glucose and store it. Glucagon makes the liver release glucose.
layers.expert: Beta cell glucose sensing triggers insulin exocytosis; insulin binds RTK, activating PI3K-Akt and GLUT4 translocation; glucagon via GPCR-cAMP-PKA stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; fasting glucose ≈ 4-5.5 mmol/L.

did_you_know: The same loop design (sensor, controller, effector) is used for body temperature, calcium and blood pressure.

steps.title: Blood sugar rises
steps.text: Digestion of a meal releases glucose into the blood.

steps.title: Sensing
steps.text: Pancreatic beta cells detect higher glucose.

steps.title: Insulin release
steps.text: Beta cells secrete insulin into the blood.

steps.title: Uptake and storage
steps.text: Muscle and fat take up glucose, the liver stores glycogen.

steps.title: Feedback
steps.text: Glucose falls, switching insulin release off.

steps.title: Counter-regulation
steps.text: If glucose gets too low, alpha cells release glucagon and the liver releases glucose.

title: Cellular respiration
summary: Cells extract energy from glucose using oxygen to make ATP.

layers.basics: Your cells burn sugar with oxygen, but in slow controlled steps that capture energy as ATP.
layers.deeper: Glycolysis in the cytosol splits glucose; the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain in mitochondria produce most ATP.
layers.expert: Glucose + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O; net ≈ 30-32 ATP per glucose (modern estimates); glycolysis yields 2 ATP + 2 NADH; TCA cycle yields NADH/FADH2; electron transport pumps protons, ATP synthase makes ATP.

did_you_know: You make and use roughly your body weight in ATP each day.

steps.title: Glycolysis
steps.text: Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol, producing a little ATP and NADH.

steps.title: Entering the mitochondrion
steps.text: Pyruvate enters mitochondria and becomes acetyl-CoA.

steps.title: Citric acid cycle
steps.text: The cycle strips electrons from acetyl-CoA into NADH and FADH2 and releases CO2.

steps.title: Electron transport
steps.text: Electrons flow through membrane complexes, pumping protons out.

steps.title: ATP synthase
steps.text: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, a spinning turbine making ATP.

steps.title: Without oxygen
steps.text: When oxygen is short, cells use fermentation to lactate for quick but lower ATP yields.

title: Protein synthesis (transcription and translation)
summary: DNA is copied into mRNA, which ribosomes read to build a protein.

layers.basics: The cell copies a gene into a messenger molecule, then ribosomes read the message three letters at a time and link amino acids into a protein.
layers.deeper: Transcription happens in the nucleus; mRNA is processed (cap, splice, tail) and exported; translation happens at ribosomes with tRNAs delivering amino acids.
layers.expert: RNA polymerase II transcribes; spliceosome removes introns (≈ 90% of a gene's length); ribosome decodes 64 codons (61 sense) via tRNA anticodon pairing; start AUG; peptide ≈ 3-6 aa/s; chaperones fold proteins.

did_you_know: Almost all life uses essentially the same genetic code.

steps.title: Unzip a gene
steps.text: RNA polymerase binds a gene's promoter and separates the DNA strands.

steps.title: Transcription
steps.text: It builds a complementary mRNA strand from the template.

steps.title: Processing
steps.text: The mRNA is capped, spliced and tailed, then exported through a nuclear pore.

steps.title: Translation start
steps.text: A ribosome binds mRNA and finds the start codon AUG.

steps.title: Elongation
steps.text: tRNAs bring amino acids matching each codon and the ribosome links them.

steps.title: Folding and delivery
steps.text: The new protein folds, may enter the ER, be modified in the Golgi and shipped.

title: Mitosis (cell division)
summary: A cell copies its chromosomes and splits into two identical daughter cells.

layers.basics: Before dividing a cell copies its DNA. Mitosis then sorts the copies equally into two new cells.
layers.deeper: Phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
layers.expert: Cyclin-CDK control; spindle assembly checkpoint; cohesin cleavage by separase triggers anaphase; centrosomes and microtubules segregate 46 chromosomes; M-phase ≈ 1 h in a ≈ 24 h cycle.

did_you_know: Your body makes millions of new cells every second by cell division.

steps.title: Prophase
steps.text: Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms.

steps.title: Metaphase
steps.text: Chromosomes line up at the cell's equator.

steps.title: Anaphase
steps.text: Sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite poles.

steps.title: Telophase
steps.text: New nuclear envelopes form around each set.

steps.title: Cytokinesis
steps.text: An actin ring pinches the cell into two.

title: Bone remodeling
summary: Old bone is steadily dissolved and replaced with new bone.

layers.basics: Your bones are constantly renewed: some cells remove old bone and others lay down new bone.
layers.deeper: Osteoclasts resorb bone; osteoblasts then fill the cavity with new matrix. Exercise and hormones regulate the balance.
layers.expert: Basic multicellular unit: activation, resorption (≈ 2-4 weeks), reversal, formation (≈ 3-4 months); RANKL/OPG, PTH, calcitriol, estrogens, sclerostin; osteoporosis arises from resorption exceeding formation.

did_you_know: Astronauts lose bone mass fast in microgravity because bone remodels in response to load.

steps.title: Sensing
steps.text: Osteocytes detect strain and microdamage.

steps.title: Activation
steps.text: Signals recruit osteoclast precursors.

steps.title: Resorption
steps.text: Osteoclasts dissolve mineral and matrix.

steps.title: Formation
steps.text: Osteoblasts lay down osteoid and mineralize it.

steps.title: Maturation
steps.text: Some osteoblasts become osteocytes; surface cells rest.

steps.title: Hormonal control
steps.text: PTH raises blood calcium by increasing resorption; calcitonin and estrogens oppose it.

title: Vision (phototransduction)
summary: Light is focused onto the retina and turned into nerve signals.

layers.basics: The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, whose cells convert it into electrical signals sent to the brain.
layers.deeper: Rods and cones contain a pigment which changes shape when hit by a photon, setting off a chemical cascade.
layers.expert: In darkness photoreceptors are depolarized and release glutamate; a photon isomerizes 11-cis to all-trans retinal, activating transducin and PDE6, reducing cGMP, closing CNG channels and hyperpolarizing the cell; ganglion cells fire to the LGN and V1.

did_you_know: Vision begins with a single molecule flipping shape in about 200 femtoseconds.

steps.title: Focusing
steps.text: The cornea bends most light and the lens fine-tunes focus.

steps.title: Image on the retina
steps.text: An inverted image forms across the retina; the fovea captures fine detail.

steps.title: Phototransduction
steps.text: A photon flips retinal in rod or cone pigment, starting an enzyme cascade.

steps.title: Signal processing
steps.text: Bipolar and ganglion cells compare and compress signals.

steps.title: To the brain
steps.text: Optic nerve fibers carry spikes to the thalamus and occipital cortex.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.text: Visual cortex builds edges, color, motion and objects.

title: Thermoregulation
summary: Body temperature is held near 37 C by balancing heat production and loss.

layers.basics: When you get hot you sweat and your skin flushes; when cold, you shiver and your skin vessels narrow.
layers.deeper: The hypothalamus acts as a thermostat, comparing set point with inputs from skin and core temperature sensors.
layers.expert: Heat loss via radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation; vasomotor control through sympathetic tone; shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis (UCP1); fever is a raised set point mediated by prostaglandin E2.

did_you_know: Evaporating one liter of sweat removes about 2,400 kJ of heat.

steps.title: Sensing
steps.text: Thermoreceptors in skin and the hypothalamus detect temperature.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.text: The hypothalamus compares to its set point.

steps.title: If too hot
steps.text: Skin vessels dilate and sweat glands release sweat.

steps.title: If too cold
steps.text: Skin vessels constrict, hair stands up, muscles shiver.

steps.title: Fever
steps.text: Pyrogens raise the set point so the body feels cold until it reaches a higher temperature.
